scenes.title: SSH & Working with Remote Servers
scenes.narration: SSH lets you securely log in to a distant server and control it as if you were sitting right in front of it.

scenes.title: What SSH Gives You
bullets: An encrypted connection so nobody can eavesdrop on your session.
A full remote shell for running commands on machines anywhere in the world.
Key-based login that is both more secure and more convenient than passwords.
scenes.narration: SSH wraps your entire session in encryption, keeping credentials and commands private even over the open internet. It hands you a real shell on the remote host, so administering a cloud server feels no different from working locally. And with key pairs you can log in without typing a password every time, which is safer and faster.

scenes.title: Connecting and Copying
scenes.code:
ssh data@server.example.com        # log in
ssh -i ~/.ssh/mykey.pem ubuntu@host # use a key file
scp report.csv data@host:/data/     # copy up
scp data@host:/data/out.csv .       # copy down
scenes.narration: The basic ssh command takes a username and host and drops you into a remote shell. Adding -i points at a private key file, which is how most cloud servers authenticate you. The scp command copies files over that same secure channel, uploading when the remote path comes second and downloading when it comes first.

scenes.title: How Key Authentication Works
steps: public key goes on the server
scenes.narration: You generate a matched pair of keys with ssh-keygen. The public half is placed on the server while the private half never leaves your machine. When you connect, the server challenges you and only your private key can answer correctly, proving your identity without a password.

scenes.text: Never share your private key or commit it to Git — treat it like the password to every server it can reach.
scenes.narration: Your private key is the master key to every server that trusts it. Guard it carefully, and never let it slip into a repository or a shared drive.
